newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO set to present Bosnia military plans.
newsitem.headline: NATO set to present Bosnia military plans.

text.p: NATO, bolstered by Washington's decision to stay on in Bosnia, is set to call on Monday for an international force of about 30,000 troops to remain in the troubled country to help cement a fragile peace.

Ambassadors from the 16-nation alliance meeting in Brussels are widely expected to endorse a middle ground option for retaining a military presence in Bosnia after the mandate for NATO's Implementation Force (IFOR) ends on December 20.

"The new force will have an essentially deterrent role and will be more involved in the civilian aspects of the peace," said one NATO diplomat. "But there is no question (of a police role) to hunt down alleged war criminals."

Although many IFOR countries are keen to stay in Bosnia to ensure the fragile peace process continues, the announcement on Friday by newly re-elected President Bill Clinton that the United States will take part all but sealed the deal.
Clinton said Washington was willing to commit about 8,500 troops to the region, reviewing the situation every six months and aiming for a final U.S. withdrawal by June 1998.
The total force is expected to contain between 25,000 and 30,000. Germany is expected to commit about 3,000 troops, France in the region of 2,500, a two-thirds reduction.
It would be the first use of German troops in a potential combat role outside the NATO area since the end of World War Two.
At its height, IFOR had about 60,000 troops, up to 20,000 of them American.

The U.S. originally insisted it would leave Bosnia at the end of the IFOR mandate, but like other states now accepts that while much progress has been made in restoring peace, the situation is far from stable.
"The Bosnian people are far better off than they were a year ago," Clinton said on Friday. "Bosnia's bitter harvest of hatred, however, has not disappeared."
Carl Bildt, the former Swedish prime minister who is the international community's representative in Bosnia, has warned that "war would break out in the blink of an eye" if IFOR pulled out now.

NATO's ambassadors, who agree the political policy for the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, are due to discuss four options for next year, ranging from leaving things exactly as they are to withdrawing completely.
They are almost certain to endorse a plan to keep the reduced force in Bosnia, with a slightly different focus, that of helping stabilise fledgling institutions.
One task will be to make it possible for delayed municipal elections to take place, probably around mid-year.

Officials say the relative success of government elections in September and the accompanying development of governent structures mean far fewer troops will be needed to see that municipal elections go smoothly.

Visiting NATO last week, Robert Frowick, head of the Organisation for Cooperation and Security in Europe (OSCE) mission to Bosnia, said strong military support was essential, adding that around 30,000 troops would be "ample."
